summary: The Cheras were one of the three crowned dynasties of the ancient Tamil country, ruling the Kerala coast and the Kongu interior from Vanchi-Karur and growing rich on the pepper that Roman and Arab ships bought at Muziris. Their power faded after the 3rd century, but a medieval Chera kingdom, the Perumals of Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur), arose c. 844 and ruled central Kerala for almost three centuries. Chola invasions from c. 988 forced it into submission, and in the early 12th century it dissolved into local kingdoms such as Venad.

details: The Cheras are among the earliest South Indian powers named in writing. The rock edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, carved in the mid-3rd century BCE, list the peoples beyond his frontiers, among them the Cholas, the Pandyas and the 'Kedalaputo', the Cheras. They lay outside his empire and are treated as friendly neighbours. Historians usually date the Chera state from this time, although some argue that in these early centuries the Cheras were a group of chiefdoms rather than a fully formed kingdom, with branches ruling from the Kerala coast and from Karur inland.

The Chera coast grew black pepper and other spices that the Roman world prized. In the 1st century CE the Greek sailing guide known as the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described Muziris, near the mouth of the Periyar river, as a port frequented by Roman, Arab and Greek ships, and Pliny the Elder also wrote about the Cheras. Spices were exchanged for Roman gold, and Roman coins and amphorae have been found at the Chera capital Karur and at Pattanam on the coast. The Cheras even counter-struck Roman silver coins with their own marks.

Two nearly identical Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in a rock shelter at Pugalur, near Karur, dated to about the 2nd century CE, are among the best evidence for the early Chera kings. They record a rock shelter made for a Jain monk named Chenkayapan and name three generations of rulers: Athan Cheral Irumporai, Perum Kadungon and Ilam Kadungo. They confirm that kings of the Irumporai branch ruled from Karur, in the Kongu country, while a western branch held the coast around Muziris. The two branches probably competed for leadership of the Chera realm.

Senguttuvan, called 'Kadal Pirakottiya', is the most celebrated of the early Chera kings praised in the Sangam anthology Pathitruppathu, and he appears in the Tamil epic Silappathikaram. The epic links him to the Sri Lankan king Gajabahu, and this synchronism is the main reason historians date him and his line to the 2nd century CE, though the method rests on guesswork. Other kings of the same age are credited in the poems with conquering the Kongu country and defeating combined Pandya and Chola armies, although praise poetry of this kind is hard to verify.

Wars among the three crowned Tamil kings were frequent. In the early 3rd century, by the usual reconstruction of the Sangam rulers, the Chera king Mantharam Cheral Irumporai, who governed a large territory, was captured by the Pandya king Nedunjeliyan II, although he later escaped. Nedunjeliyan is remembered for a victory at Talaiyalanganam over the forces of the Chera and Chola kings. Such defeats weakened the Irumporai Cheras of Karur at the very end of the Sangam age, after which Chera power went into a long decline.

Between the 3rd and 5th centuries the power of the early Cheras declined sharply, and the history of their lands becomes poorly documented. The Cheras of Karur, sometimes called the Keralas, seem to have kept a hold on part of the former Chera territory. Across the Tamil country the Kalabhras displaced the old royal houses, and later the region fell under the domination of the Chalukyas, Pallavas and Pandyas, then the Rashtrakutas and Cholas. For more than five centuries no strong Chera kingdom is recorded on the Kerala coast.

In the 8th or 9th century central Kerala separated from the older Chera realm in the Kongu country and formed a new kingdom whose kings were called Perumals. Its capital was Mahodayapuram, also called Makotai, at modern Kodungallur near the ancient port of Muziris. The earliest known king, Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara, began to reign around 844. He was allied with the Chola king Aditya I and is credited with helping the Cholas win the western Tamil country in the late 9th century. The new kings claimed descent from the ancient Cheras.

In about 849, the fifth year of Sthanu Ravi, Ayyan Adikal, the chieftain of Venad in the far south, issued a grant to the Christian merchant Mar Sapir Iso for the Tarisappalli church at Kollam (Quilon). It gave land and bonded workers to the church and made two merchant guilds, the Anjuvannam and the Manigramam, tenants of the settlement, with tax privileges. Witnesses signed in Arabic, Middle Persian and Judeo-Persian. It is the oldest surviving inscription of the medieval Chera kingdom and shows Christian, Jewish and Muslim traders at work on its coast.

For over a century the Perumals were allies of the Cholas, and King Vijayaraga married his daughters to the Chola king Parantaka I. That changed under Rajaraja I, perhaps because the Cholas wanted to break the Chera hold on the pepper trade. His earliest inscriptions celebrate a triumph at Kandalur Salai, near modern Thiruvananthapuram, around 988, and his general captured the port of Vizhinjam. Chola inscriptions appear in Kanyakumari district in the 990s and in the Thiruvananthapuram area by the early 1000s, as the southern Chera lands slipped from Perumal control.

Bhaskara Ravi, who ruled from about 962 to 1021, issued a copper-plate charter at Muyirikode, near his capital, to Joseph Rabban, a Jewish merchant magnate of Kodungallur. It gave Rabban the rights of the Anjuvannam merchant guild, including toll and customs privileges, and made them hereditary for his descendants. Historians date it to about 1000. Some think the grant rewarded Jewish merchants for financial or military help to the Chera state at a time of Chola threats. Cochin's Jewish community long treasured the plates as the deed of their settlement.

Chola pressure turned into conquest. A Chola inscription at Senur dated 1005 boasts of the destruction of the Pandya capital, Madurai, and the defeat of the rulers of Kollam, Kolla-desham and Kodungallur, the Chera capital. The Chola subjugation of Kerala is dated to the early years of the 11th century. Under Rajaraja's son Rajendra I, Chola control over Kerala became firm, and the land was held for a time as an appanage for junior Chola princes. The Perumal kings survived, but as subordinates of the Cholas.

The Chola king Kulottunga I brought the Chera and Pandya lands back under Chola control in campaigns of 1077 to 1081, and Chola forces pushed north to Kollam around 1097. The last Perumal, Rama Kulasekhara, crowned around 1089, reportedly retook the city around 1102 and used it as a second headquarters. An inscription at the Rameswaram temple in Kollam, dated 1102, records a council at which the king publicly atoned for wrongs against Brahmins, an unusual act for a ruling Chera. Chola campaigns in south Kerala continued until about 1118.

A Chola inscription from Thanjavur dated 1122 mentions 'the flight of the Chera king to the sea'. Rama Kulasekhara's reign ended in the early 1120s, and with it the medieval Chera kingdom dissolved into several local powers; historians see changing land relations as a key cause, as local Nair leaders took over the running of temples. Tradition holds that his son Vira Kerala became the first independent ruler of Venad in the south, while the rulers of Kozhikode and Kochi rose elsewhere. A popular legend says the last Cheraman Perumal divided his kingdom and left for Mecca.
